title: Greg Sherwood MW: Franschhoek’s wine story is better than it thinks
summary:
It’s a common problem for journalists, critics and commentators based in Europe when visiting the Cape winelands – Stellenbosch and the near surrounding winelands, seem to always command a magnetic draw, a vinous tractor beam a la Star Wars, that pulls you in and does not release you until you only have one or two […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Franschhoek’s wine story is better than it thinks appeared first on winemag.
content:
It’s a common problem for journalists, critics and commentators based in Europe when visiting the Cape winelands – Stellenbosch and the near surrounding winelands, seem to always command a magnetic draw, a vinous tractor beam a la Star Wars, that pulls you in and does not release you until you only have one or two days left of your broader visit schedule.

The ‘casualties’ are normally the more far-flung wine regions that are slightly tricky for a quick day trip or tasting when staying in Cape Town (or even Stellenbosch), especially when there is an indulgent liquid-heavy producer lunch or dinner thrown into the mix. I’m talking the Swartland, Elgin, Franschhoek and especially the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley.

Fortunately, on my recent trip to the Cape to judge for the Michelangelo Wine & Spirit Awards, I decided to make a conscious effort to schedule some meaningful wine time for several days after judging in both Franschhoek and the Hemel-en-Aarde / Walker Bay regions. As I know all too well from regularly tasting small new project wines from young Elsenburg graduates or from the next generation of ‘young gun’ producers, exciting things are always taking place right under your nose… but often don’t get the credit and attention they deserve.

Working in co-ordination with the Franschhoek Vignerons’ membership, and in particular Gerard Holden of Holden Manz winery fame, I was able to put together an incredibly in-depth, deep-dive line-up of wine tastings, vineyard walks and winery visits over a three-day visit in Franschhoek.

Franschhoek is of course better known as the “French Corner” of the Cape winelands, and as such, has built up an internationally respected reputation for boutique wine quality to accompany its world-famous culinary tourism and boutique hotel and spa scene. Yet the region’s wineries have faced uneven success when it comes to growing sales volumes of their wines not only in the UK, historically South Africa’s largest export market, but also further afield in the EU and USA.

Undoubtedly, the Franschhoek Valley and its vignerons are not exactly short on brand strengths and general unique selling points when it comes to promoting their wider reputation. They already possess a brand equity built on quality and heritage, with their unique Huguenot founding story and French lineage intertwined with a well-established food-and-wine tourism identity helping to set them apart from other nearby regions such as Paarl, Wellington, and indeed Stellenbosch.

This distinct narrative advantage over other generic “South African wines” has given the Valley a valuable differentiated positioning in the UK market where South Africa is already a familiar, trusted Wine of Origin for international consumers. Crucially for the Franschhoek Valley, South African wine exports have been shifting from bulk to value added, an export strategy that has been prioritised by multiple wine industry trade bodies for some years now, where market diversification and strategic positioning have become all important.

As global wine consumption continues to soften, the data reveals that volumes shipped to the UK declined by 7% in the most recent reporting period, while export value rose by 4%, underscoring the growing competitiveness of South African wine in retail and on-trade channels.

For Franschhoek’s largely premium, packaged-wine producers, this “value over volume” trend plays directly to their strengths as they are not competing on bulk pricing but on quality, story and provenance, which the market is rewarding even as overall demand contracts.

Somewhat paradoxically, as an outsider, in the past I have still continued to sense a certain insecurity, or perhaps ‘chip on the shoulder’ from many Franschhoek wineries when it comes to comparing their wines’ quality and reputation to the wider market. The zenith of this insecurity probably peaked a few years ago when a number of Franschhoek producers expressed an interest in being reclassified under a Wine of Origin Paarl umbrella.

As someone who has bought, sold and drunk the best wines of Franschhoek for many decades, I can only attribute this frail insecurity indirectly to the Valley’s overriding global reputation as primarily the home of many ‘money is no object’ lifestyle winery estates where boutique spas, restaurants, and hotel luxury trumped the importance of vine health and wine quality.

But let me reassure both consumers and producers – after three deep dive days tasting and travelling around the Valley, I’m happy to report that this is a completely outdated perception that perhaps held some sway 20 or 30 years ago but should now be put firmly to bed in the face of a tsunamic of premium wine offerings made, in many cases, by a new generation of young, ambitious winemakers.

Franschhoek’s wine problem isn’t quality

Some industry commentators still refer to the Franschhoek Valley’s pressing weakness as its lake of scale. Franschhoek is a small Ward, and production is largely boutique within the context of the Western Cape wine industry. Most estates lack the production volumes to supply UK multiple grocers at the price points and consistency those retailers demand, with 71% of producers considered small-scale, crushing between 1 and 500 tons of grapes annually.

This natural limit on Franschhoek producers’ ability to fulfill large retail contracts without blending across regions, has potentially led in recent years to a slight dilution of ‘Brand Franschhoek’ and its global identity.

But looking at the ongoing general demographic movement and evolution in the wider international wine market with lower consumption trends but at higher premium price points, small estates in Franschhoek, many of whom rely exclusively on specialty importers and agents for their UK sales and distribution, might just find themselves and their niche wine brands in the right place at the right time.

Another overlooked benefit of decades of luxury tourism to the Valley is how this now plays directly into the fast growing Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) sales trend, with these channels now emerging as quite lucrative alternative revenue streams for wineries at higher-than-normal margins.

Despite volume pressures, the UK remains the anchor market in which South Africa cannot afford to lose momentum, and the opportunity is there to deepen value rather than chase volume. With UK wine imports from South Africa bigger than Germany, the Netherlands and the USA combined, taken together with UK tourist numbers to the Cape topping US visitor numbers once again (after a post-COVID jump), the importance, scale and value of existing relationships should not be underestimated.

To my mind, there is still plenty of room for Franschhoek’s producers to leverage more aggressively through premiumisation, positioning single-estate, terroir-driven wines above the generic South African category, in specialist independents, fine-dining lists, and DTC subscription models. As always, wine tourism – while not a be-all and end-all opportunity in itself – remains an underused lever for converting cellar-door visitors into meaningful UK customers.

Just this week, Robert Joseph, the renowned UK wine industry journalist, commentator, and at times, ‘hard truths wine sleuth’, wrote an article on LinkedIn titled “Turning Visitors Into Customers” revealing some interesting numbers coming out of Bordeaux with regards to tourism after his conversations with a prominent tour guide who runs visits primarily to top Chateaux.

Quoting some truly fabulous (and hilarious) German words to illustrate his point, like ‘Schatzblindheit’ (treasure blindness); ‘Chancenblindheit’ (opportunity blindness); as well as ‘Hilfeannahmeverweigerung’ (refusal to help), these terms seemed perfectly appropriate descriptors of a phenomenon in Bordeaux, where Chateaux received well informed guests and poured them €25 to €75 samples of wine without so much as collecting one single visitors’ name, email or social media handle. Not once.

As Robert concludes… “Allowing wine drinkers to visit your winery, without at the very least trying to obtain some means of remaining in contact with them, makes absolutely no sense in 2026.”

While the Franschhoek Valley wineries, unlike Bordeaux who have both volume and quality, are unlikely to win a UK or EU volume war, and almost certainly shouldn’t try, their realistic path to continued success will be value-led, premiumising the Franschhoek Valley name, expanding direct-to-consumer and hospitality channels, and better exploiting the very well establish fine dining and culinary USP of the Franschhoek Valley, tying the boutique wines of the Valley more closely into a premium virtuous food and wine circle.

The data and market demographic shifts suggest the market is already rewarding this approach, with value growing as volumes shrink, and Franschhoek’s quality-tourism identity is well placed to help drive the popularity of the Valley’s quality wines long into the future.

Footnote:  On my recent trip, I want to thank all the Vignerons who generously gave me their time to taste and chat about the current state of play in the beautiful Franschhoek Valley: Anthonij Rupert Wines, Babylonstoren, Chamonix, Great Heart, Haute Cabrière, Holden Manz, La Bri, La Motte, Le Lude, Lynx, Old Road Wine Co., Paserene, Rickety Bridge, Stony Brook, Terre Paisible, and Wildeberg.

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

title: Michael Fridjhon: Wine scores haven’t failed – we’ve debased them
summary:
Christian Eedes’s recent piece on judging, scoring and the role of the critic was a masterly summary of the issues being debated in the admittedly rarefied space where people ponder arcane concerns about wine and wine aesthetics (and which needless to say probably don’t bother most wine drinkers). In what is an unconnected but not […]

The post Michael Fridjhon: Wine scores haven’t failed – we’ve debased them appeared first on winemag.
content:
Christian Eedes’s recent piece on judging, scoring and the role of the critic was a masterly summary of the issues being debated in the admittedly rarefied space where people ponder arcane concerns about wine and wine aesthetics (and which needless to say probably don’t bother most wine drinkers). In what is an unconnected but not unrelated piece on Substack, Lloyd Jusa (chief somm at The Saxon) tilted at the Michelin burgundy ratings (a target larger and comfortably more deserving of the joust than Don Quixote’s windmills).

Eedes’s article fell naturally into two parts – the difficulty with the scoring system and the impossibility of incorporating the complexity of fine wine into a few digits. The first part is easiest to deal with, but no less fruitless. Partly his article was a lament about something many of us have been hammering on about for some time, namely score inflation. The solution however is not recalibration – that horse has long ago bolted and anyway was never ever properly in the paddock.

When a currency devalues (in other words, is the victim of inflation) it can be recalibrated: in 1960 France created the New Franc, worth 100 of the Old Francs. It may have been a shock to the citizens, but they had no choice about using it and quickly discovered that it meant working with fewer noughts at the end of the prices. In the early days of the Trophy Wine Show we had an effective spread of 50 points in our version of the 100 point system. We knew what we were doing – and even the overseas judges swiftly adjusted to it. But consumers were at sea with it. With wine there’s no central bank, no ultimate arbiter of scores, to benchmark values or to force a recalibration of a system which has been abused by critics who promote themselves by nudging the scores ever higher (and by producers whose addiction to inflated scores fuels the debasement of the currency).

Over the years many people have decried the idea that a score can communicate the nuanced complexity of wine. Does the Mona Lisa qualify for 100 and the Guernica 97? How do you rate a Jackson Pollock? Is Hamlet only worth a 93 (too many corpses on the stage at the end of Act Five – in which case what to make of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey?) Hugh Johnson felt that a star rating system was less prescriptive. Michel Bettane, a supremely fine taster (and formerly an academic) used to drive us mad in the early days of the Trophy Wine Show by grading wines with α or β or even β- (in the end he succumbed to the 100 point system because subscribers to Bettane + Desseauve wanted hard numbers).

Parker’s success with the 100 point system was a comforting enhancement for wine drinkers (especially first generation wine drinkers) when it became popular in the 1980s. They understood the American university grading system so it conveyed something meaningful to them, and to an extent it survived score inflation for a time because the American college system was also undergoing the same experience. (My son who graduated from Columbia a year ago regarded an A- as a catastrophe. I’m pretty certain that students in the 1980s would not have reacted in the same way.)

I don’t think that numerical scoring (so probably the 100 point system) is going to vanish anytime soon, even if its usefulness continues to diminish. It will serve to provide a broad guide to quality, an indication that a wine is safe to drink. It won’t induce purchase the way it used to in the days when a 100 point score was so rare that it guaranteed a sellout, or a Platter Five Star was a boast worth making. And it hasn’t become irrelevant because our wines have become better, or because wines all over the world are technically better than they were 40 years ago. It’s become irrelevant for the same reason that the French had to abandon the Old Franc – because it’s worth shit.

The more important question arising from the Winemag editorial remains unanswered: how do we communicate meaningfully about wine in a way which is fair both to the wine and to the consumer seeking to make a purchase? We need to think carefully about the language we use: too many adjectives, mostly linked to primary fruit notes, often unfamiliar to the average reader, are simply not helpful. (Greg Sherwood MW and I have sparred about this a few times). You wouldn’t go to a play on the strength of a review which said “Splendid, awe-inspiring, brilliant, tense, dramatic, breath-taking.” You expect the critic to be less over-the-top, more precise, thoughtful, nuanced. You need to believe that he/she understands theatre – so comments on the direction, the use of the stage, the aesthetics, are as important as insights into the performances.

But we also need to determine which wines deserve this kind of detail. There are fewer and fewer bad wines, a vast number of very good (but not life-changing) wines, and still only a handful worth “worth the trip” (to use the Guide Michelin’s definition of a Three Star dining establishment). I haven’t tasted all of the 15 wines which Eedes said had scored 97 points or more over the course of the last month. However, I’m willing to bet that not all (not even the majority) were life-changing. Scoring – and especially high scores – are a flawed way of summarising a wine review, but they have only become useless because, like the boy who used to “cry wolf” they can no longer be believed.

  • Michael Fridjhon has over thirty-five years’ experience in the liquor industry. He is the founder of Winewizard.co.za and holds various positions including Visiting Professor of Wine Business at the University of Cape Town; founder and director of WineX – the largest consumer wine show in the Southern Hemisphere and chairman of The Trophy Wine Show.

title: Tim James: The story of semillon (white and red) in the Cape
summary:
What is probably the world’s newest grape variety (for a while at least) has its past firmly rooted in three centuries or more of Cape winemaking. As reported last week, the world’s first officially certified sémillon gris vineyard is thriving at the Roundstone estate of Mullineux in the Swartland. No other vineyard in the world […]

The post Tim James: The story of semillon (white and red) in the Cape appeared first on winemag.
content:
What is probably the world’s newest grape variety (for a while at least) has its past firmly rooted in three centuries or more of Cape winemaking. As reported last week, the world’s first officially certified sémillon gris vineyard is thriving at the Roundstone estate of Mullineux in the Swartland. No other vineyard in the world can, as yet, claim the grape, though the official mother block is derived (via a long process of propagation and evaluation) from the “red semillon” vines on an old Swartland vineyard – and there are other such vines scattered around the Cape, mostly interplanted with what is now the dominant variety of semillon in the Cape, the standard white version.

Given this, it seemed a good idea to look at what we know of the story of red semillon in the Cape, including revived interest in it this century. I’ve been interested in the topic for some time – and can probably claim my own small “first”: I’d guess that my 2009 article in World of Fine Wine. “Red Semillon: Return of the wine grape” was the first substantial journalistic report on the gris version. I’d been prompted in this research by having recently seen red semillon vines for the first time, at the mixed ‘T Voetpad vineyard from which Eben Sadie was that year making a wine, which would help bring attention to the variety.

The rise of the Cape’s “wine grape”

The much-cited figure of 93% as the proportion of semillon in the Cape vineyard in the 1820s comes from an estimate made by civil servant William Bird in his “State of the Cape of Good Hope in 1822”. He was referrring to “the common green grape”, or groendruif – so common that it was often simply called wijndruif, or “wine grape”. (The colour reference was apparently to the bright foliage, not to the grape.) It gained this dominance in the context of a huge expansion of Cape vineyards following the British occupation in 1795 and later full colonial ownership. In 1795 there were about a million vines in the Cape; in 1822 Bird estimated 22 million. Groendruif was obviously the easiest to grow in various ways, including resistance to the dominant diseases.

What we don’t know is when the mutation that produced “red greengrape” happened. It could have been a century or more earlier, any time since semillon was first planted here (probably imported by Van Riebeek in 1653). But by the time Bird was writing red greengrape was already common. The great viticulturist Abraham Perold published some historical notes in the 1930s, which quoted evidence given in 1826 by farmers to an official wine-trade committee (Perold translated them from the Dutch). A Paarl farmer said that most of his 100 000 vines were interplanted red and white greengrape: “For ordinary wine I […] crush the red and white Greengrape together in order to equalize the colour and taste.” And a Stellenbosch farmer only had greengrape, “all of the same age, about 12 years”. But, crucially, he refers to “ordinary and white Greengrape”, implying that the red version was predominant and regarded as the more basic.

It was probably the vineyard destruction caused by phylloxera in the last decades of the 19th century that most prompted a major change in plantings and hugely reduced the predominance of greengrape. It was only about half of the vineyard at the turn of the century, and its presence continued to decline.

From greengrape to Sémillon

The identification with semillon came only later in the 20th century – I don’t know exactly how and when (and would be very grateful to learn this, and to know the first Cape wine with the name on the label). Perold in 1927 writes in his Treatise on Viticulture of the white and red versions of greengrape, and mentions two types of the white – one “worthless”, one better and agreeing ”very closely with the Sémillon of Sauternes”. But he says he hadn’t been able to determine greengrape’s identity.

Someone already had, however, at least to his own satisfaction. One of my wine heroes, J P de Waal, manager of Groot Constantia, while making an international wine study tour had apparently noted in Bordeaux that white greengrape is identical to semillon. But nothing came of this observation (reference to which I came across in an obscure book); no doubt de Waal would have taken it further had he not been accidentally killed on the same tour.  By the time C J Orffer wrote his little book on Wine Grape Cultivars in South Africa in 1979, the relevant section is entitled “Sémillon (Greengrape)” and it reports that greengrape is a clonal variation of the semillon of south-western France. The plantings were down to just 3.4% of the total. Orffer makes no mention of the red version; nor does Platter in his description of semillon in his 1980 Guide.

Red semillon/greengrape lingered on here and there in older vineyards, however, interplanted with the white. It was in this century, as interest grew in the Cape’s viticultural heritage, that significant attention started being paid to these remnants. In my 2009 article I mentioned (and now forget the source) that Nigel McNaught at Stony Brook had made a few vintages of a dessert wine from the red version. McNaught guessed that about a tenth of Franschhoek’s old bushvine semillon was red at the time. And in Wellington, Graham Knox of Stormhoek in 2006 took cuttings from the red-fruited vines amongst his semillon to plant a small new vineyard – but that was, sadly, fairly soon lost.

I also elsewhere noted that that, probably in the wake of the attention brought by the Sadie/Rosa Kruger explorations and winemaking, Pieter Euvrard of the Orangerie farm on the Paardeberg had bottled some wine from red semillon for his sadly short-lived wine-label of that name. In fact, I reported in my book of 2013 that this “was certainly the first bottle of wine labeled Red Semillon” – but that was my mistake, unless it was uncertified, as the authorities would never have allowed a then-non-existent variety to be credited on a label.

And so to Franziska Wickens’s planting of a red semillon vineyard in 2013, and Andrea Mullineux’s maiden vintage in the same year of The Gris for the CWG Auction, made from the red semillon vines on a 1960-planted Paardeberg vineyard. Chris and Andrea Mullineux had started working with that vineyard in 2012, and had immediately taken the cuttings which inaugurated the lengthy process of propagation, evaluation and, eventually, the establishment of the semillon gris vineyard on their Roundstone farm. It’s this vineyard that is the basis on which, first, the local authorities recognised semillon gris as a distinct variety, to be followed by the formal recognition of the OIV (International Organisation of Vine and Wine) via its International List of Vine Varieties.

It seems to me a rather nice coincidence that this vineyard was planted in 2022 – exactly two centuries after the famous report on the great predominance of semillon in the Cape.  And the first wine off the young vines was made in 2025, the centenary of  Abraham Perold’s planting of the first seeds from his experimental crossing of cinsaut and pinot noir. I happily drank a few glasses of it with Andrea recently (it was predictably gorgeous) – it’s intended to be offered for the CWG auction next year, replacing “The Gris” Old Vine Sémillon with, of course, Sémillon Gris, the first, and so far only, wine allowed to carry that name.

A note on the name

A brief note on the accented e, etc: The official name in France (and South Africa) is sémillon. Here, as in Australia for example, the accent is frequently dropped, which the authorities seem to allow even on labels. Journalistically, it’s seldom included here – as in this article, except when I’m quoting directly or using the full French name (so it admittedly looks a bit of a muddle). Mullineux has always used the accent. As for the capital letter, that’s also generally treated as a matter of house style. And the official name is Sémillon Gris – very French; but it’ll take me a while at least to stop referring casually to red semillon.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Mullineux revives historic Cape grape Sémillon Gris
summary:
A forgotten piece of Cape wine history has been given a new lease on life. After more than a decade of selection, propagation and certification, Sémillon Gris has been recognised internationally as a distinct grape variety, with Mullineux establishing the world’s first officially certified Sémillon Gris vineyard at their Roundstone property in the Swartland. The […]

The post Mullineux revives historic Cape grape Sémillon Gris appeared first on winemag.
content:
A forgotten piece of Cape wine history has been given a new lease on life. After more than a decade of selection, propagation and certification, Sémillon Gris has been recognised internationally as a distinct grape variety, with Mullineux establishing the world’s first officially certified Sémillon Gris vineyard at their Roundstone property in the Swartland.

The near-hectare vineyard represents the culmination of work led by Andrea and Chris Mullineux, together with viticultural specialists and industry bodies, to preserve and formally establish a grape that has been part of the Cape’s history for centuries.

Sémillon arrived in the Cape in the 17th century and, by the 19th century, was one of the region’s dominant varieties. Known locally as Groendruif, it once accounted for the vast majority of Cape plantings. Over time, a natural pink-skinned mutation emerged in vineyards alongside Sémillon Blanc. Known as Rooi Groendruif or Sémillon Gris, it was harvested and vinified together with the white-skinned form and was never formally recognised as a separate variety.

As vineyard replanting accelerated after phylloxera, Sémillon Gris gradually disappeared, surviving only in isolated old vineyards. Interest in the variety grew as South Africa’s wine industry began looking more closely at historic vines and varieties that had adapted to local conditions over generations.

The Mullineux project began in 2012 in a dry-farmed Swartland vineyard planted in 1960, where Sémillon Blanc and Sémillon Gris still grew together. Selected vines were propagated in collaboration with Vititec, SAWIS and the Department of Agriculture, with the certified mother block established at Roundstone in 2022.

The vineyard has now been entered on the International List of Vine Varieties of the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV) as a distinct variety, giving Sémillon Gris formal international recognition for the first time.

Mullineux has worked with Sémillon Gris for more than a decade through its Cape Winemakers Guild auction wine “The Gris”, made from selected grapes in an old Swartland vineyard where the variety was not yet officially recognised.

Future releases from Roundstone will be among the first wines in the world able to carry the Sémillon Gris name officially, turning a once-overlooked mutation into a recognised part of South Africa’s viticultural heritage.

The post Prescient Cabernet Sauvignon Report 2026: Rules and entry form appeared first on winemag.
content:
Rules

  • Wines must contain a minimum of 85% Cabernet Sauvignon and be certified as South African.
  • Wines entered must be current release or soon to be released (minimum stock requirement: 100 x 6 bottles). Producers may enter as many different wines as they see fit.
  • An entry sample takes the form of two bottles. There are two submission methods – please indicate the number corresponding to your chosen option on the entry form: 
    1. collection by Aspiring Couriers (login and create a waybill here)
    2. delivery to Aspiring Couriers
  • Entries close Wednesday 2 September. The deadline for the submission of samples is 17h00 on Thursday 3 September. LATE SUBMISSIONS WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED.
  • In the event a wine achieves Top 10 status, 18 bottles must be set aside at no charge, these to be served at promotional events.

To enter, kindly ensure you (or the company you represent) are a subscriber to Winemag.co.za. If you’re not yet subscribed, click here to sign up.

An entry fee of R1,495 including VAT per wine applies and you will be directed to our online shop to make payment after you have completed the entry form below. Please note that if you want to enter multiple wines, each will require a separate form although payment can be made all at once.

The post Prescient Cape Bordeaux Red Blend Report 2026: Rules and entry form appeared first on winemag.
content:
Rules

  • Wines must be certified as South African. Only Bordeaux-style red blends will be accepted, with the style defined as wines made from two or more of the following varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Merlot and Petit Verdot (NO OTHER VARIETIES PERMITTED).

  • Wines entered must be current release or soon to be released (minimum stock requirement: 100 x 6 bottles). Producers may enter as many different wines as they see fit.

title: Greg Sherwood MW: Franschhoek’s wine story is better than it thinks
summary:
It’s a common problem for journalists, critics and commentators based in Europe when visiting the Cape winelands – Stellenbosch and the near surrounding winelands, seem to always command a magnetic draw, a vinous tractor beam a la Star Wars, that pulls you in and does not release you until you only have one or two […]

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Franschhoek’s wine story is better than it thinks appeared first on winemag.
content:
It’s a common problem for journalists, critics and commentators based in Europe when visiting the Cape winelands – Stellenbosch and the near surrounding winelands, seem to always command a magnetic draw, a vinous tractor beam a la Star Wars, that pulls you in and does not release you until you only have one or two days left of your broader visit schedule.

The ‘casualties’ are normally the more far-flung wine regions that are slightly tricky for a quick day trip or tasting when staying in Cape Town (or even Stellenbosch), especially when there is an indulgent liquid-heavy producer lunch or dinner thrown into the mix. I’m talking the Swartland, Elgin, Franschhoek and especially the Hemel-en-Aarde Valley.

Fortunately, on my recent trip to the Cape to judge for the Michelangelo Wine & Spirit Awards, I decided to make a conscious effort to schedule some meaningful wine time for several days after judging in both Franschhoek and the Hemel-en-Aarde / Walker Bay regions. As I know all too well from regularly tasting small new project wines from young Elsenburg graduates or from the next generation of ‘young gun’ producers, exciting things are always taking place right under your nose… but often don’t get the credit and attention they deserve.

Working in co-ordination with the Franschhoek Vignerons’ membership, and in particular Gerard Holden of Holden Manz winery fame, I was able to put together an incredibly in-depth, deep-dive line-up of wine tastings, vineyard walks and winery visits over a three-day visit in Franschhoek.

Franschhoek is of course better known as the “French Corner” of the Cape winelands, and as such, has built up an internationally respected reputation for boutique wine quality to accompany its world-famous culinary tourism and boutique hotel and spa scene. Yet the region’s wineries have faced uneven success when it comes to growing sales volumes of their wines not only in the UK, historically South Africa’s largest export market, but also further afield in the EU and USA.

Undoubtedly, the Franschhoek Valley and its vignerons are not exactly short on brand strengths and general unique selling points when it comes to promoting their wider reputation. They already possess a brand equity built on quality and heritage, with their unique Huguenot founding story and French lineage intertwined with a well-established food-and-wine tourism identity helping to set them apart from other nearby regions such as Paarl, Wellington, and indeed Stellenbosch.

This distinct narrative advantage over other generic “South African wines” has given the Valley a valuable differentiated positioning in the UK market where South Africa is already a familiar, trusted Wine of Origin for international consumers. Crucially for the Franschhoek Valley, South African wine exports have been shifting from bulk to value added, an export strategy that has been prioritised by multiple wine industry trade bodies for some years now, where market diversification and strategic positioning have become all important.

As global wine consumption continues to soften, the data reveals that volumes shipped to the UK declined by 7% in the most recent reporting period, while export value rose by 4%, underscoring the growing competitiveness of South African wine in retail and on-trade channels.

For Franschhoek’s largely premium, packaged-wine producers, this “value over volume” trend plays directly to their strengths as they are not competing on bulk pricing but on quality, story and provenance, which the market is rewarding even as overall demand contracts.

Somewhat paradoxically, as an outsider, in the past I have still continued to sense a certain insecurity, or perhaps ‘chip on the shoulder’ from many Franschhoek wineries when it comes to comparing their wines’ quality and reputation to the wider market. The zenith of this insecurity probably peaked a few years ago when a number of Franschhoek producers expressed an interest in being reclassified under a Wine of Origin Paarl umbrella.

As someone who has bought, sold and drunk the best wines of Franschhoek for many decades, I can only attribute this frail insecurity indirectly to the Valley’s overriding global reputation as primarily the home of many ‘money is no object’ lifestyle winery estates where boutique spas, restaurants, and hotel luxury trumped the importance of vine health and wine quality.

But let me reassure both consumers and producers – after three deep dive days tasting and travelling around the Valley, I’m happy to report that this is a completely outdated perception that perhaps held some sway 20 or 30 years ago but should now be put firmly to bed in the face of a tsunamic of premium wine offerings made, in many cases, by a new generation of young, ambitious winemakers.

Franschhoek’s wine problem isn’t quality

Some industry commentators still refer to the Franschhoek Valley’s pressing weakness as its lake of scale. Franschhoek is a small Ward, and production is largely boutique within the context of the Western Cape wine industry. Most estates lack the production volumes to supply UK multiple grocers at the price points and consistency those retailers demand, with 71% of producers considered small-scale, crushing between 1 and 500 tons of grapes annually.

This natural limit on Franschhoek producers’ ability to fulfill large retail contracts without blending across regions, has potentially led in recent years to a slight dilution of ‘Brand Franschhoek’ and its global identity.

But looking at the ongoing general demographic movement and evolution in the wider international wine market with lower consumption trends but at higher premium price points, small estates in Franschhoek, many of whom rely exclusively on specialty importers and agents for their UK sales and distribution, might just find themselves and their niche wine brands in the right place at the right time.

Another overlooked benefit of decades of luxury tourism to the Valley is how this now plays directly into the fast growing Direct-to-Consumer (DTC) sales trend, with these channels now emerging as quite lucrative alternative revenue streams for wineries at higher-than-normal margins.

Despite volume pressures, the UK remains the anchor market in which South Africa cannot afford to lose momentum, and the opportunity is there to deepen value rather than chase volume. With UK wine imports from South Africa bigger than Germany, the Netherlands and the USA combined, taken together with UK tourist numbers to the Cape topping US visitor numbers once again (after a post-COVID jump), the importance, scale and value of existing relationships should not be underestimated.

To my mind, there is still plenty of room for Franschhoek’s producers to leverage more aggressively through premiumisation, positioning single-estate, terroir-driven wines above the generic South African category, in specialist independents, fine-dining lists, and DTC subscription models. As always, wine tourism – while not a be-all and end-all opportunity in itself – remains an underused lever for converting cellar-door visitors into meaningful UK customers.

Just this week, Robert Joseph, the renowned UK wine industry journalist, commentator, and at times, ‘hard truths wine sleuth’, wrote an article on LinkedIn titled “Turning Visitors Into Customers” revealing some interesting numbers coming out of Bordeaux with regards to tourism after his conversations with a prominent tour guide who runs visits primarily to top Chateaux.

Quoting some truly fabulous (and hilarious) German words to illustrate his point, like ‘Schatzblindheit’ (treasure blindness); ‘Chancenblindheit’ (opportunity blindness); as well as ‘Hilfeannahmeverweigerung’ (refusal to help), these terms seemed perfectly appropriate descriptors of a phenomenon in Bordeaux, where Chateaux received well informed guests and poured them €25 to €75 samples of wine without so much as collecting one single visitors’ name, email or social media handle. Not once.

As Robert concludes… “Allowing wine drinkers to visit your winery, without at the very least trying to obtain some means of remaining in contact with them, makes absolutely no sense in 2026.”

While the Franschhoek Valley wineries, unlike Bordeaux who have both volume and quality, are unlikely to win a UK or EU volume war, and almost certainly shouldn’t try, their realistic path to continued success will be value-led, premiumising the Franschhoek Valley name, expanding direct-to-consumer and hospitality channels, and better exploiting the very well establish fine dining and culinary USP of the Franschhoek Valley, tying the boutique wines of the Valley more closely into a premium virtuous food and wine circle.

The data and market demographic shifts suggest the market is already rewarding this approach, with value growing as volumes shrink, and Franschhoek’s quality-tourism identity is well placed to help drive the popularity of the Valley’s quality wines long into the future.

Footnote:  On my recent trip, I want to thank all the Vignerons who generously gave me their time to taste and chat about the current state of play in the beautiful Franschhoek Valley: Anthonij Rupert Wines, Babylonstoren, Chamonix, Great Heart, Haute Cabrière, Holden Manz, La Bri, La Motte, Le Lude, Lynx, Old Road Wine Co., Paserene, Rickety Bridge, Stony Brook, Terre Paisible, and Wildeberg.

  • Greg Sherwood was born in Pretoria, South Africa, and as the son of a career diplomat, spent his first 21 years traveling the globe with his parents. With a Business Management and Marketing degree from Webster University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA, Sherwood began his working career as a commodity trader. In 2000, he decided to make more of a long-held interest in wine taking a position at Handford Wines in South Kensington, London, working his way up to the position of Senior Wine Buyer over 22 years. Sherwood currently consults to a number of top fine wine merchants in London while always keeping one eye firmly on the South African wine industry. He qualified as the 303rd Master of Wine in 2007.

The post Greg Sherwood MW: Franschhoek’s wine story is better than it thinks appeared first on winemag.

title: Michael Fridjhon: Wine scores haven’t failed – we’ve debased them
summary:
Christian Eedes’s recent piece on judging, scoring and the role of the critic was a masterly summary of the issues being debated in the admittedly rarefied space where people ponder arcane concerns about wine and wine aesthetics (and which needless to say probably don’t bother most wine drinkers). In what is an unconnected but not […]

The post Michael Fridjhon: Wine scores haven’t failed – we’ve debased them appeared first on winemag.
content:
Christian Eedes’s recent piece on judging, scoring and the role of the critic was a masterly summary of the issues being debated in the admittedly rarefied space where people ponder arcane concerns about wine and wine aesthetics (and which needless to say probably don’t bother most wine drinkers). In what is an unconnected but not unrelated piece on Substack, Lloyd Jusa (chief somm at The Saxon) tilted at the Michelin burgundy ratings (a target larger and comfortably more deserving of the joust than Don Quixote’s windmills).

Eedes’s article fell naturally into two parts – the difficulty with the scoring system and the impossibility of incorporating the complexity of fine wine into a few digits. The first part is easiest to deal with, but no less fruitless. Partly his article was a lament about something many of us have been hammering on about for some time, namely score inflation. The solution however is not recalibration – that horse has long ago bolted and anyway was never ever properly in the paddock.

When a currency devalues (in other words, is the victim of inflation) it can be recalibrated: in 1960 France created the New Franc, worth 100 of the Old Francs. It may have been a shock to the citizens, but they had no choice about using it and quickly discovered that it meant working with fewer noughts at the end of the prices. In the early days of the Trophy Wine Show we had an effective spread of 50 points in our version of the 100 point system. We knew what we were doing – and even the overseas judges swiftly adjusted to it. But consumers were at sea with it. With wine there’s no central bank, no ultimate arbiter of scores, to benchmark values or to force a recalibration of a system which has been abused by critics who promote themselves by nudging the scores ever higher (and by producers whose addiction to inflated scores fuels the debasement of the currency).

Over the years many people have decried the idea that a score can communicate the nuanced complexity of wine. Does the Mona Lisa qualify for 100 and the Guernica 97? How do you rate a Jackson Pollock? Is Hamlet only worth a 93 (too many corpses on the stage at the end of Act Five – in which case what to make of Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey?) Hugh Johnson felt that a star rating system was less prescriptive. Michel Bettane, a supremely fine taster (and formerly an academic) used to drive us mad in the early days of the Trophy Wine Show by grading wines with α or β or even β- (in the end he succumbed to the 100 point system because subscribers to Bettane + Desseauve wanted hard numbers).

Parker’s success with the 100 point system was a comforting enhancement for wine drinkers (especially first generation wine drinkers) when it became popular in the 1980s. They understood the American university grading system so it conveyed something meaningful to them, and to an extent it survived score inflation for a time because the American college system was also undergoing the same experience. (My son who graduated from Columbia a year ago regarded an A- as a catastrophe. I’m pretty certain that students in the 1980s would not have reacted in the same way.)

I don’t think that numerical scoring (so probably the 100 point system) is going to vanish anytime soon, even if its usefulness continues to diminish. It will serve to provide a broad guide to quality, an indication that a wine is safe to drink. It won’t induce purchase the way it used to in the days when a 100 point score was so rare that it guaranteed a sellout, or a Platter Five Star was a boast worth making. And it hasn’t become irrelevant because our wines have become better, or because wines all over the world are technically better than they were 40 years ago. It’s become irrelevant for the same reason that the French had to abandon the Old Franc – because it’s worth shit.

The more important question arising from the Winemag editorial remains unanswered: how do we communicate meaningfully about wine in a way which is fair both to the wine and to the consumer seeking to make a purchase? We need to think carefully about the language we use: too many adjectives, mostly linked to primary fruit notes, often unfamiliar to the average reader, are simply not helpful. (Greg Sherwood MW and I have sparred about this a few times). You wouldn’t go to a play on the strength of a review which said “Splendid, awe-inspiring, brilliant, tense, dramatic, breath-taking.” You expect the critic to be less over-the-top, more precise, thoughtful, nuanced. You need to believe that he/she understands theatre – so comments on the direction, the use of the stage, the aesthetics, are as important as insights into the performances.

But we also need to determine which wines deserve this kind of detail. There are fewer and fewer bad wines, a vast number of very good (but not life-changing) wines, and still only a handful worth “worth the trip” (to use the Guide Michelin’s definition of a Three Star dining establishment). I haven’t tasted all of the 15 wines which Eedes said had scored 97 points or more over the course of the last month. However, I’m willing to bet that not all (not even the majority) were life-changing. Scoring – and especially high scores – are a flawed way of summarising a wine review, but they have only become useless because, like the boy who used to “cry wolf” they can no longer be believed.

  • Michael Fridjhon has over thirty-five years’ experience in the liquor industry. He is the founder of Winewizard.co.za and holds various positions including Visiting Professor of Wine Business at the University of Cape Town; founder and director of WineX – the largest consumer wine show in the Southern Hemisphere and chairman of The Trophy Wine Show.

The post Michael Fridjhon: Wine scores haven’t failed – we’ve debased them appeared first on winemag.

title: Tim James: The story of semillon (white and red) in the Cape
summary:
What is probably the world’s newest grape variety (for a while at least) has its past firmly rooted in three centuries or more of Cape winemaking. As reported last week, the world’s first officially certified sémillon gris vineyard is thriving at the Roundstone estate of Mullineux in the Swartland. No other vineyard in the world […]

The post Tim James: The story of semillon (white and red) in the Cape appeared first on winemag.
content:
What is probably the world’s newest grape variety (for a while at least) has its past firmly rooted in three centuries or more of Cape winemaking. As reported last week, the world’s first officially certified sémillon gris vineyard is thriving at the Roundstone estate of Mullineux in the Swartland. No other vineyard in the world can, as yet, claim the grape, though the official mother block is derived (via a long process of propagation and evaluation) from the “red semillon” vines on an old Swartland vineyard – and there are other such vines scattered around the Cape, mostly interplanted with what is now the dominant variety of semillon in the Cape, the standard white version.

Given this, it seemed a good idea to look at what we know of the story of red semillon in the Cape, including revived interest in it this century. I’ve been interested in the topic for some time – and can probably claim my own small “first”: I’d guess that my 2009 article in World of Fine Wine. “Red Semillon: Return of the wine grape” was the first substantial journalistic report on the gris version. I’d been prompted in this research by having recently seen red semillon vines for the first time, at the mixed ‘T Voetpad vineyard from which Eben Sadie was that year making a wine, which would help bring attention to the variety.

The rise of the Cape’s “wine grape”

The much-cited figure of 93% as the proportion of semillon in the Cape vineyard in the 1820s comes from an estimate made by civil servant William Bird in his “State of the Cape of Good Hope in 1822”. He was referrring to “the common green grape”, or groendruif – so common that it was often simply called wijndruif, or “wine grape”. (The colour reference was apparently to the bright foliage, not to the grape.) It gained this dominance in the context of a huge expansion of Cape vineyards following the British occupation in 1795 and later full colonial ownership. In 1795 there were about a million vines in the Cape; in 1822 Bird estimated 22 million. Groendruif was obviously the easiest to grow in various ways, including resistance to the dominant diseases.

What we don’t know is when the mutation that produced “red greengrape” happened. It could have been a century or more earlier, any time since semillon was first planted here (probably imported by Van Riebeek in 1653). But by the time Bird was writing red greengrape was already common. The great viticulturist Abraham Perold published some historical notes in the 1930s, which quoted evidence given in 1826 by farmers to an official wine-trade committee (Perold translated them from the Dutch). A Paarl farmer said that most of his 100 000 vines were interplanted red and white greengrape: “For ordinary wine I […] crush the red and white Greengrape together in order to equalize the colour and taste.” And a Stellenbosch farmer only had greengrape, “all of the same age, about 12 years”. But, crucially, he refers to “ordinary and white Greengrape”, implying that the red version was predominant and regarded as the more basic.

It was probably the vineyard destruction caused by phylloxera in the last decades of the 19th century that most prompted a major change in plantings and hugely reduced the predominance of greengrape. It was only about half of the vineyard at the turn of the century, and its presence continued to decline.

From greengrape to Sémillon

The identification with semillon came only later in the 20th century – I don’t know exactly how and when (and would be very grateful to learn this, and to know the first Cape wine with the name on the label). Perold in 1927 writes in his Treatise on Viticulture of the white and red versions of greengrape, and mentions two types of the white – one “worthless”, one better and agreeing ”very closely with the Sémillon of Sauternes”. But he says he hadn’t been able to determine greengrape’s identity.

Someone already had, however, at least to his own satisfaction. One of my wine heroes, J P de Waal, manager of Groot Constantia, while making an international wine study tour had apparently noted in Bordeaux that white greengrape is identical to semillon. But nothing came of this observation (reference to which I came across in an obscure book); no doubt de Waal would have taken it further had he not been accidentally killed on the same tour.  By the time C J Orffer wrote his little book on Wine Grape Cultivars in South Africa in 1979, the relevant section is entitled “Sémillon (Greengrape)” and it reports that greengrape is a clonal variation of the semillon of south-western France. The plantings were down to just 3.4% of the total. Orffer makes no mention of the red version; nor does Platter in his description of semillon in his 1980 Guide.

Red semillon/greengrape lingered on here and there in older vineyards, however, interplanted with the white. It was in this century, as interest grew in the Cape’s viticultural heritage, that significant attention started being paid to these remnants. In my 2009 article I mentioned (and now forget the source) that Nigel McNaught at Stony Brook had made a few vintages of a dessert wine from the red version. McNaught guessed that about a tenth of Franschhoek’s old bushvine semillon was red at the time. And in Wellington, Graham Knox of Stormhoek in 2006 took cuttings from the red-fruited vines amongst his semillon to plant a small new vineyard – but that was, sadly, fairly soon lost.

I also elsewhere noted that that, probably in the wake of the attention brought by the Sadie/Rosa Kruger explorations and winemaking, Pieter Euvrard of the Orangerie farm on the Paardeberg had bottled some wine from red semillon for his sadly short-lived wine-label of that name. In fact, I reported in my book of 2013 that this “was certainly the first bottle of wine labeled Red Semillon” – but that was my mistake, unless it was uncertified, as the authorities would never have allowed a then-non-existent variety to be credited on a label.

And so to Franziska Wickens’s planting of a red semillon vineyard in 2013, and Andrea Mullineux’s maiden vintage in the same year of The Gris for the CWG Auction, made from the red semillon vines on a 1960-planted Paardeberg vineyard. Chris and Andrea Mullineux had started working with that vineyard in 2012, and had immediately taken the cuttings which inaugurated the lengthy process of propagation, evaluation and, eventually, the establishment of the semillon gris vineyard on their Roundstone farm. It’s this vineyard that is the basis on which, first, the local authorities recognised semillon gris as a distinct variety, to be followed by the formal recognition of the OIV (International Organisation of Vine and Wine) via its International List of Vine Varieties.

It seems to me a rather nice coincidence that this vineyard was planted in 2022 – exactly two centuries after the famous report on the great predominance of semillon in the Cape.  And the first wine off the young vines was made in 2025, the centenary of  Abraham Perold’s planting of the first seeds from his experimental crossing of cinsaut and pinot noir. I happily drank a few glasses of it with Andrea recently (it was predictably gorgeous) – it’s intended to be offered for the CWG auction next year, replacing “The Gris” Old Vine Sémillon with, of course, Sémillon Gris, the first, and so far only, wine allowed to carry that name.

A note on the name

A brief note on the accented e, etc: The official name in France (and South Africa) is sémillon. Here, as in Australia for example, the accent is frequently dropped, which the authorities seem to allow even on labels. Journalistically, it’s seldom included here – as in this article, except when I’m quoting directly or using the full French name (so it admittedly looks a bit of a muddle). Mullineux has always used the accent. As for the capital letter, that’s also generally treated as a matter of house style. And the official name is Sémillon Gris – very French; but it’ll take me a while at least to stop referring casually to red semillon.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Mullineux revives historic Cape grape Sémillon Gris
summary:
A forgotten piece of Cape wine history has been given a new lease on life. After more than a decade of selection, propagation and certification, Sémillon Gris has been recognised internationally as a distinct grape variety, with Mullineux establishing the world’s first officially certified Sémillon Gris vineyard at their Roundstone property in the Swartland. The […]

The post Mullineux revives historic Cape grape Sémillon Gris appeared first on winemag.
content:
A forgotten piece of Cape wine history has been given a new lease on life. After more than a decade of selection, propagation and certification, Sémillon Gris has been recognised internationally as a distinct grape variety, with Mullineux establishing the world’s first officially certified Sémillon Gris vineyard at their Roundstone property in the Swartland.

The near-hectare vineyard represents the culmination of work led by Andrea and Chris Mullineux, together with viticultural specialists and industry bodies, to preserve and formally establish a grape that has been part of the Cape’s history for centuries.

Sémillon arrived in the Cape in the 17th century and, by the 19th century, was one of the region’s dominant varieties. Known locally as Groendruif, it once accounted for the vast majority of Cape plantings. Over time, a natural pink-skinned mutation emerged in vineyards alongside Sémillon Blanc. Known as Rooi Groendruif or Sémillon Gris, it was harvested and vinified together with the white-skinned form and was never formally recognised as a separate variety.

As vineyard replanting accelerated after phylloxera, Sémillon Gris gradually disappeared, surviving only in isolated old vineyards. Interest in the variety grew as South Africa’s wine industry began looking more closely at historic vines and varieties that had adapted to local conditions over generations.

The Mullineux project began in 2012 in a dry-farmed Swartland vineyard planted in 1960, where Sémillon Blanc and Sémillon Gris still grew together. Selected vines were propagated in collaboration with Vititec, SAWIS and the Department of Agriculture, with the certified mother block established at Roundstone in 2022.

The vineyard has now been entered on the International List of Vine Varieties of the International Organisation of Vine and Wine (OIV) as a distinct variety, giving Sémillon Gris formal international recognition for the first time.

Mullineux has worked with Sémillon Gris for more than a decade through its Cape Winemakers Guild auction wine “The Gris”, made from selected grapes in an old Swartland vineyard where the variety was not yet officially recognised.

Future releases from Roundstone will be among the first wines in the world able to carry the Sémillon Gris name officially, turning a once-overlooked mutation into a recognised part of South Africa’s viticultural heritage.

The post Prescient Cabernet Sauvignon Report 2026: Rules and entry form appeared first on winemag.
content:
Rules

  • Wines must contain a minimum of 85% Cabernet Sauvignon and be certified as South African.
  • Wines entered must be current release or soon to be released (minimum stock requirement: 100 x 6 bottles). Producers may enter as many different wines as they see fit.
  • An entry sample takes the form of two bottles. There are two submission methods – please indicate the number corresponding to your chosen option on the entry form: 
    1. collection by Aspiring Couriers (login and create a waybill here)
    2. delivery to Aspiring Couriers
  • Entries close Wednesday 2 September. The deadline for the submission of samples is 17h00 on Thursday 3 September. LATE SUBMISSIONS WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED.
  • In the event a wine achieves Top 10 status, 18 bottles must be set aside at no charge, these to be served at promotional events.

To enter, kindly ensure you (or the company you represent) are a subscriber to Winemag.co.za. If you’re not yet subscribed, click here to sign up.

An entry fee of R1,495 including VAT per wine applies and you will be directed to our online shop to make payment after you have completed the entry form below. Please note that if you want to enter multiple wines, each will require a separate form although payment can be made all at once.
